html:
The Swift Creek culture was a Middle Woodland people of the Southeast of North America, living from about 100 to 800 CE in what is now Georgia, Alabama, Florida, South Carolina and Tennessee. It is named after the Swift Creek mound site in Bibb County, Georgia, near Macon.

Swift Creek people built mounds and buried their dead with care, but most did not live in one place all year. They hunted, fished and gathered. They are best known for their pottery, pressed with carved wooden paddles that left swirling, curving designs.

Archaeologists call them "Hopewellian": they were part of the wide Hopewell exchange world. Pottery stamped with the same diamond checks turns up at Hopewell sites in Ohio and Indiana and at Crystal River in Florida. In Florida their ceremonial and burial customs are called the Yent and Green Point complex. Neighbours on the map in these centuries include Copena, Porter and the Marksville culture. In northwest Florida the Weeden Island culture grew out of Swift Creek.
